passages.t: Grain picked on the Sabbath: Lord of the Sabbath
passages.happening:
On a Sabbath, Jesus walks through the grainfields. His disciples are hungry, so they pick heads of grain and eat them. Some Pharisees see it and say, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.”

Jesus gives three answers. First, David: when he and his men were hungry, they ate the consecrated bread that only priests were allowed to eat. Second, the priests: every Sabbath they work in the temple, and yet they are innocent. “But I tell you that something greater than the temple is here.” Third, the prophet Hosea: “If only you had known the meaning of ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent. For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story too (Mark 2:23-28), and the note there explains the background. The Law let a hungry traveller pick grain by hand from a neighbour's field (Deuteronomy 23:25). The problem was the day. Jewish teachers worked hard to define what counted as work, so that people could keep the Sabbath faithfully. Their later rulings, written down around AD 200 in the Mishnah, list thirty-nine kinds of work, with reaping and threshing among them. Picking grain and rubbing it in the hands looked like a small harvest.

Matthew tells it a little differently. Only he says the disciples were hungry, which makes Jesus' point about David sharper. He leaves out the name of the priest, Abiathar, which Mark gives. He also leaves out Mark's saying “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). In its place he adds two arguments a Jewish teacher would respect: the priests' work in the temple, and Hosea 6:6.

The Sabbath was not a burden God invented to test his people. It was a gift: one day in seven when slaves, servants, animals and masters all stopped. The Pharisees loved it and wanted to guard it. That is what makes the argument serious. Both sides cared about the same day.

In Greek, ‘something greater’ is a neuter word, meizon, not ‘someone’. Readers take it as Jesus himself, or as the presence of God at work in him. Either way, it is a staggering claim. The temple was the holiest place in the world to a Jew. Jesus says that what is happening in him is greater.
passages.ot:
David's story is in 1 Samuel 21:1-6. Running from King Saul, he was given “the Bread of the Presence,” twelve loaves that the Law reserved for the priests (Leviticus 24:5-9).

The priests' Sabbath work is in the Law too. Every Sabbath they offered extra sacrifices: “two unblemished year-old male lambs” as well as the daily offering (Numbers 28:9-10). Killing, carrying and burning were all work, yet the temple's service came before the Sabbath rest. If the temple could do that, Jesus says, so can something greater than the temple.

Hosea 6:6 is the verse Jesus already quoted to the Pharisees at Matthew's dinner (9:13): “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.” Matthew is the only Gospel to quote it, and he quotes it twice.

The Sabbath itself goes back to creation (Genesis 2:3) and to the exodus: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). It was always meant as mercy.
passages.hard:
Did Jesus do away with the Sabbath? He says he is its Lord, not its enemy. In the same Gospel he says, “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (5:17).

Christians have understood the Sabbath in more than one way, and these notes do not choose between them. Many keep Sunday, the day of the resurrection, as the Lord's Day and a Christian day of rest and worship. Some, such as Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists, keep the seventh day, Saturday. Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ himself, who gives rest (11:28), and point to Paul: “let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath” (Colossians 2:16). Hebrews says, “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). All agree that rest is God's gift and that Jesus is its Lord.

It is also unfair to make the Pharisees cartoon villains here. They asked a real question about God's law. Jesus' answer comes from inside Israel's own Scriptures, from David, the priests and Hosea. It is an argument among Jews about what God's day is for.
passages.asks: The disciples were hungry, and the critics saw only a broken rule. Ask whether your faith has more room for rules than for people. And ask what your week looks like. Is there a day when you stop and rest, trusting God to hold the world without you? The Sabbath was made as a gift.

passages.t: A withered hand healed on the Sabbath
passages.happening:
Jesus goes into their synagogue. A man with a withered hand is there. To find a charge against Jesus, they ask him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”

Jesus answers with a question. If one of you has a sheep that falls into a pit on the Sabbath, won't you take hold of it and lift it out? “How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” Then he tells the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretches it out, and it is restored, just like the other. But the Pharisees go out and plot how they might kill Jesus.
passages.hearers:
Jewish teaching holds that saving a life comes before the Sabbath. The clearest early statement is in the Mishnah, written down around AD 200, so later than the Gospels: where there is even a doubt whether a life is in danger, the Sabbath gives way (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). The question was how far to go in lesser cases.

On animals, opinions differed. A rule book called the Damascus Document, known from copies among the Dead Sea Scrolls, forbids lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath. Other Jewish teachers were less strict. Jesus' question assumes that most of the people listening would pull their sheep out. A sheep was money and food. Nobody would leave it to die.

The man's hand was not an emergency. He could have waited until sunset, when the Sabbath ended. That is why the case was a test. Jesus' answer moves the question. It is not only ‘what is allowed?’ but ‘what is good?’ To leave a person in need when you could help is not neutral.

Mark tells the same story (Mark 3:1-6) and says Jesus looked at them with anger and sorrow. Matthew leaves out the feelings and the Herodians, and adds the sheep in the pit. In both Gospels the ending is the same. Jesus gives a man back his hand, and on the same day his opponents begin planning a death.
passages.ot:
The Sabbath law says “you must keep My Sabbaths, for this will be a sign between Me and you” (Exodus 31:13). No commandment in the Law forbids healing. The question was how to keep the command, not whether to keep it.

The Law also cared for animals in trouble. If you saw your neighbour's ox or sheep straying, or his donkey or ox fallen on the road, you were not to ignore it (Deuteronomy 22:1-4). Jesus argues from the smaller case to the greater, a way of reasoning Jewish teachers often used: if a sheep, how much more a man.
passages.hard:
Was Jesus breaking the Law? Matthew does not think so. Jesus never says the Sabbath does not matter. He says healing is ‘lawful’, which means allowed by God's law rightly read. He argues as a Jewish teacher, from Scripture and from common practice, about what the Law means.

It is fair to the Pharisees to say that they were not cruel men who hated healing. They feared that if the Sabbath was bent for every good cause, it would soon mean nothing. Jesus' answer is that doing good is not bending the Sabbath. It is keeping it as God meant it. The tragedy of the scene is not that they asked a question. It is that, faced with a healed man, they went out to plot.
passages.asks: ‘How much more valuable is a man than a sheep.’ Ask whether there is someone you have treated as worth less than your own comfort, your schedule, or your rules. Is there good you could do today that you have been putting off until a more convenient time?

passages.happening:
Jesus knows about the plot, so he withdraws. Large crowds follow him, and he heals them all, warning them not to make him known.

Matthew says this fulfilled what God had said through Isaiah: “Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will proclaim justice to the nations. He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets. A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish, till He leads justice to victory. In His name the nations will put their hope.”
passages.hearers:
Many in Jesus' day hoped for a Messiah who would fight. Jesus slips away from a plot instead of calling a crowd to arms. He heals people and asks them to keep quiet. Matthew explains this with Isaiah's picture of God's Servant, who wins quietly.

The two pictures are from ordinary life. A reed was a cheap, hollow stem, used for a pen or a measuring rod. Once it was cracked, people snapped it and threw it away. A wick was a twist of flax in a small oil lamp. When it began to smoke and sputter, you pinched it out. Isaiah's Servant does neither. He does not throw away what is damaged. He does not put out what is nearly out.

Notice who comes into view. ‘The nations’ means the Gentiles, the non-Jewish peoples. The quotation names them twice. Matthew has already shown Gentiles coming to Jesus, the wise men (2:1-12) and the Roman officer (8:5-13), and it will end with the disciples sent to ‘all nations’ (28:19).
passages.ot:
The quotation is Isaiah 42:1-4. Matthew's wording is not exactly the same as Isaiah's in English Bibles. Isaiah's last line reads “In His law the islands will put their hope” (Isaiah 42:4). Matthew gives it as ‘In His name the nations will put their hope’. Matthew often gives Old Testament words in a form that brings out what he sees fulfilled.

Hearers would catch an echo from earlier in the book. At Jesus' baptism the voice from heaven said, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (3:17). The quotation here calls the Servant ‘My beloved, in whom My soul delights’ and says ‘I will put My Spirit on Him’. The Spirit came down on Jesus at that baptism. The Servant Isaiah described is the Son God named.
passages.asks: Is there a part of you that feels like a bruised reed or a wick about to go out? Worn thin by grief, failure, doubt, or simply years of trying? This passage says Jesus does not snap the cracked reed. Ask whether you have believed that he would. And ask how you treat the bruised people around you: do you finish them off, or do you shelter the flame?

passages.t: The Beelzebul accusation and the strong man
passages.happening:
A man who is demon-possessed, blind and mute is brought to Jesus, and Jesus heals him so that he can see and speak. The crowds are astonished. They ask, “Could this be the Son of David?”

The Pharisees hear and say, “Only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, does this man drive out demons.” Jesus knows what they are thinking. A kingdom divided against itself is ruined. If Satan drives out Satan, how can his kingdom stand? And “if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out?” But if he drives them out by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon them. No one can rob a strong man's house unless he first ties up the strong man. Then Jesus says, “He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.”
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this argument too (Mark 3:22-30), and the note there explains the name. Beelzebul goes back to Baal-zebub, “the god of Ekron” (2 Kings 1:2). Many scholars think the older form meant something like ‘prince Baal’ or ‘lord of the exalted house’. By Jesus' day it was a name for the chief of the evil spirits. If ‘zebul’ does mean house, Jesus' answer about a divided house and a strong man's house plays on it.

Matthew adds a few things. He begins with a healing, so the reader sees exactly what the Pharisees are calling evil: a blind and mute man made whole. He adds the crowd's question, ‘Son of David?’, a title for the Messiah. And he adds ‘your sons’, the Pharisees' own followers.

Other Jews did drive out demons in those days. The historian Josephus tells of a Jew named Eleazar who freed possessed people in front of the Roman general Vespasian. He held a ring with a root to the person's nose and spoke incantations said to come from King Solomon (Antiquities 8.46-48). Jesus' point is simple. If you call my exorcisms the devil's work, what will you say of your own people's? The difference with Jesus is that he needs no ring and no spell. He speaks, and the man is free.

Luke gives the saying as “the finger of God” (Luke 11:20). Matthew says ‘the Spirit of God’. Both mean that God's own power is at work.
passages.ot:
The strong man comes from Isaiah. God asks, “Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be delivered?” and answers, “Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved” (Isaiah 49:24-25). The people held by evil are the plunder. Jesus has come to take them back.

The crowd's question, ‘Son of David?’, looks back to God's promise of a king from David's line (2 Samuel 7:12-16). Some readers also recall that Solomon, the first son of David, was remembered by later Jews as a master of wisdom over spirits, as Josephus's story shows. Here is a greater son of David.
passages.hard:
“He who is not with Me is against Me” sounds like the opposite of what Jesus says in Mark: “For whoever is not against us is for us” (Mark 9:40). Which is it?

The two sayings answer different questions. In Mark, the disciples want to stop a man who drives out demons in Jesus' name but is not one of their group. Jesus says, leave him alone: anyone working in my name is on our side. Here, in Matthew, the question is about Jesus himself. When God's power is plainly at work in him, no one can stay neutral. You either gather with him or you scatter. Be generous toward others who serve Jesus; be honest about where you stand toward Jesus.

A word on illness. Matthew tells this man's blindness and silence as the work of a demon. But Matthew also lists the sick and the possessed as different needs (4:24) and tells of mute people healed with no demon mentioned (15:30-31). As the note on 9:32-34 says, the Gospel does not teach that every disability or illness has an evil spirit behind it, and it would be wrong and cruel to say so of anyone today.
passages.asks: The Pharisees saw a man healed and decided it must be evil, because they had already decided about Jesus. Ask whether you have ever refused to call something good because of who did it. And hear Jesus' last line: there is no neutral ground. Are you gathering with him, or only watching?

passages.t: The sin against the Spirit; words and the heart
passages.happening:
Then Jesus gives a solemn warning. “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.” A word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, “either in this age or in the one to come.”

He goes on to speak about trees and fruit. A good tree gives good fruit, and a bad tree bad fruit, “for a tree is known by its fruit.” He calls his opponents a “brood of vipers” and says, “out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks.” People will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they have spoken. “For by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned.”
passages.hearers:
Blasphemy meant speaking against God, insulting what is holy. It was among the gravest crimes in the Law (Leviticus 24:16).

The setting matters. The Pharisees had just watched God's Spirit set a blind and mute man free, and they had said it was the devil's work. That is what Jesus is answering. They did not misunderstand once. They looked straight at the goodness of God and called it evil.

‘Brood of vipers’ was the phrase John the Baptist had used for the same people (3:7). A viper looks harmless until it strikes. The ‘careless word’ is literally an ‘idle’ word, the Greek argos, the same word Matthew uses of the workers ‘doing nothing’ in the marketplace (20:3). It means a word that does no good, that comes out without thought. Jesus says even those words show the heart.

Matthew's version is fuller than Mark's (Mark 3:28-30). Only Matthew and Luke include the line about the Son of Man (Luke 12:10), and only Matthew adds ‘in this age or in the one to come’.
passages.ot: Jesus' words about fruit repeat what he said in the Sermon on the Mount: “every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit” (7:17). The picture runs through the Old Testament. The righteous person in Psalm 1 is like a tree “yielding its fruit in season” (Psalm 1:3). Through Jeremiah God says he searches the heart “to reward a man according to his way, by what his deeds deserve” (Jeremiah 17:10).
passages.hard:
What is the sin that will never be forgiven? If you are afraid you have committed it, this note is written for you.

In Matthew, as in Mark, the sin is defined by the setting. The Pharisees saw the plain work of God's Spirit, setting a man free, and called it the work of the devil. It is not a careless word spoken once in anger. It is a settled refusal to see God's goodness as good, a refusal that shuts the door on the very forgiveness Jesus offers. Christians have described it in more than one way. Some see it as calling the Spirit's work evil with open eyes. Many, through the long history of the church, have described it as a refusal of God's mercy held on to until the end. Some think it could be committed in its full form only by people who saw Jesus' works; others link it with the warnings in Hebrews 6:4-6. These notes state the views and do not choose.

Why can a word against the Son of Man be forgiven, but not this? Many readers suggest that who Jesus was could still be misunderstood in his humble life on earth. Paul, who once spoke against Jesus, says, “I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13). The Spirit's work in freeing the possessed was plain.

Many Christians have feared they committed this sin. In 1666 John Bunyan, later the author of The Pilgrim's Progress, described in Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners how he long feared he had committed it, and how he came at last to comfort in Christ. A long pastoral tradition answers that the fear itself is a sign that the heart has not turned hard in this way. Note too what comes first: “every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men.” The promise is wide before the warning is given.
passages.asks: Jesus says words come from the overflow of the heart. Listen to what has come out of your mouth this week, the careless words most of all. What do they say about what fills you? And if a fear of the unforgivable sin troubles you, bring it to Jesus. The one who warned also said, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened” (11:28).

passages.happening:
Some scribes and Pharisees say, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” Jesus answers, “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.

Then he names two witnesses for the judgment. The men of Nineveh repented when Jonah preached, “and now One greater than Jonah is here.” The Queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, “and now One greater than Solomon is here.”
passages.hearers:
They had just seen a blind and mute man healed. Asking for a sign now means asking for proof on their own terms, something from heaven that would force belief. Jesus refuses.

‘Adulterous’ does not mean everyone in that generation was unfaithful in marriage. The prophets described Israel's unfaithfulness to God as adultery, as if God were a husband betrayed. Through Jeremiah God says “faithless Israel had committed adultery” (Jeremiah 3:8). Jesus speaks as the prophets did, to his own generation. Christians have sometimes turned words like these against the Jewish people as a whole. That is a misuse. The warning is for every generation that sees God at work and still demands more proof, including our own.

Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that had crushed the northern kingdom of Israel. It was the last city a Jew would expect to repent. The Queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, from a land far to the south, who came to test Solomon (1 Kings 10:1). Two Gentiles, an enemy city and a foreign queen, will stand up at the judgment and put God's own people to shame. They responded to less. ‘One greater’ is here.
passages.ot:
Jonah's story is short. God sent him to preach to Nineveh. He ran the other way, was thrown into the sea, and “Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish” (Jonah 1:17). Then he went to Nineveh and preached, and “the Ninevites believed God” (Jonah 3:5).

The queen's story is in 1 Kings 10. She heard of Solomon's fame, came to see for herself, and said, “not even half was told to me” (1 Kings 10:7).

So the sign of Jonah has two sides. Jonah came back from the deep, and Jesus will come back from the grave. And Jonah's preaching brought pagans to repent, while Jesus' own people refused something greater.
passages.hard:
How could Jesus be “three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” if he died on a Friday afternoon and rose early on Sunday? By our way of counting, that is about a day and a half: part of Friday, all of Saturday, part of Sunday. In the 1790s Thomas Paine pressed this point in The Age of Reason, saying that by the Gospels' own account Jesus was in the grave only one day and two nights. Skeptics since have listed the verse as a contradiction.

The most common answer is the way people counted days. Jews often counted inclusively: any part of a day counted as the day. A teacher remembered in the Talmud, written down centuries later, Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah, is quoted as saying that a day and a night make one period, and part of the period counts as the whole. The Bible itself counts loosely. Esther asks the Jews to fast “for three days, night or day,” and goes to the king “On the third day” (Esther 4:16; 5:1). An Egyptian had gone without food “for three days and three nights” and says his master left him “three days ago” (1 Samuel 30:12-13). Matthew, who wrote this verse, also records Jesus saying he would be raised “on the third day” (16:21), and has his enemies ask for the tomb to be guarded “until the third day” because he had said ‘after three days’ (27:63-64). For Matthew the phrases meant the same span.

A minority of Christians reads the words as a full seventy-two hours and places the crucifixion on Wednesday, taking the Sabbath that followed as a festival Sabbath. Most Christians and most scholars hold the Friday date, which fits Mark's note that Jesus died on “the day before the Sabbath” (Mark 15:42). This is a question about the calendar, on which Christians differ. It is not a question about the resurrection itself, which all four Gospels and Paul proclaim: “He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4).
passages.asks: The Ninevites had one reluctant prophet and turned. The queen travelled a long way on a rumour. Ask what kind of sign you have been waiting for before you take God seriously. Jesus says the sign has already been given: one who died and came back. What more would you need, and would you believe it if it came?

passages.happening: Jesus tells a short, unsettling story. When an unclean spirit leaves a person, it wanders through dry places looking for rest and finds none. So it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.’ It comes back and finds the house empty, swept clean, and put in order. Then it brings seven other spirits worse than itself, and they move in. That person ends up worse off than before. Jesus ends: “So will it be with this wicked generation.”
passages.hearers:
The last line tells us what the story is about. It is a picture of Jesus' generation. John the Baptist had called the nation to repent, and crowds had gone out to be baptized. Jesus had driven out demons and healed in their towns. The house had been cleaned. But a clean house with no one living in it is an open door. If the people did not take in the one who was cleaning it, their last state would be worse than the first.

In the Old Testament, deserts and ruins are pictured as the home of wild and lonely creatures, the opposite of a living city (Isaiah 34:14). The spirit's ‘rest’ is a grim mirror of the rest Jesus has just offered the weary (11:28).

The point is about emptiness. Getting rid of something bad is not the same as being filled with something good. A life that is only swept and tidied, with no one at home, is not safe.
passages.hard:
Does this passage teach that illness, especially mental illness, is a spirit that can return? No. Jesus is telling a parable about a generation, and he says so (verse 45). It is not a medical teaching, and it does not mean that someone whose illness comes back has let in a demon. Illness of body or mind is illness. If something you have struggled with has returned, that is not a judgment on your faith. Please get help again: a doctor, a pastor, or a crisis line.

Nor is it meant to frighten a person who has turned to Christ. The empty house is a life that has been cleaned up but has not let Jesus in. The answer it points to is not fear but welcome: let him live there.
passages.asks: It is possible to clean up a life without letting God in: to drop a bad habit, tidy the outside, and leave the house empty. Ask what fills the space where an old sin used to be. Is your faith a set of things you have stopped doing, or a person you live with?

passages.happening:
While Jesus is still speaking to the crowds, his mother and brothers stand outside, wanting to speak to him. Someone tells him, “Look, Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to speak to You.”

Jesus replies, “Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?” Pointing to his disciples, he says, “Here are My mother and My brothers. For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.”
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 3:31-35), and the note there explains how hard these words would have landed. Family gave a person a name, a living, protection and a place. To call his followers his mother and brothers was to say a new family was being formed, not by blood but by doing God's will.

Matthew tells it with two changes. He leaves out Mark's earlier line that Jesus' family thought he was ‘out of His mind’ (Mark 3:21). And where Mark says ‘the will of God’, Matthew says ‘the will of My Father in heaven’. Jesus' family is the family of his Father.

Notice that Jesus points to his disciples. Matthew has just shown three groups: the Pharisees who reject him, his relatives who stand outside, and the disciples who are with him. The question for every reader is which group he is in.
passages.hard:
Is Jesus rejecting his mother? No. He is opening his family, not closing it. Mary herself is the first example of what he describes. When the angel came to her, she said, “I am the Lord's servant,” and “May it happen to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). In John's Gospel Jesus provides for her from the cross (John 19:26-27).

Who were his brothers? Matthew will name four of them in the next chapter (13:55-56). Christians have understood them in three ways: as later children of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view), as Joseph's children by an earlier marriage (the Orthodox view), or as cousins (a long Catholic view). The note on Matthew 13:53-58 says more. All three agree on what Jesus says here: the deepest family is the one that does the Father's will.
passages.asks: Jesus points at ordinary people and says, ‘Here is My family.’ Ask whether you are standing inside with him or outside asking him to come out to you. And if your own family has let you down, or you have none, hear this: anyone who does the Father's will is his brother and sister and mother. Who in your church needs you to be family to them?
